theme: The Samaritan woman; living water; the official’s son
readingInstruction: Read John 4:1-54. Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at a well, offers her living water, and many in her town believe. He then heals an official’s son from a distance. Notice who Jesus talks to and what he offers.
settingTheScene: Jesus leaves Judea and goes north to Galilee, taking the road through Samaria, which most Jews avoided because of centuries of hostility. At noon he sits by Jacob’s well, tired, while his disciples go to buy food. A woman comes to draw water at a time when no one else would be there. Jews and Samaritans did not share dishes, and a rabbi did not usually speak with a woman in public. Jesus breaks every barrier.
observation: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, Give me a drink, you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (4:10).
“The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (4:14).
“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?” (4:29).
“I who speak to you am he” (4:26).
“My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (4:34).
“We have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world” (4:42).
interpretation:
Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. The request surprises her. Then he turns it around: if she knew who was asking, she would ask him for living water. She thinks he means running water, but he is speaking of the Spirit, a spring welling up in a person to eternal life. The woman asks for it, perhaps still half joking, and Jesus says, “Go, call your husband.” She has had five husbands, and the man she lives with now is not her husband. Jesus knows her whole story, and he does not shrink from it. His aim is not to shame her but to bring her to the truth.

She changes the subject to the old argument over where to worship. Jesus tells her that the hour is coming, and is now here, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. We will return to this in the doctrinal pause. Then she says, “I know that Messiah is coming,” and Jesus says, “I who speak to you am he.” This is the first time in the Gospel that Jesus openly says he is the Messiah, and he says it to a Samaritan woman with a past.

She leaves her water jar and goes to the town, saying, “Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?” She is the first evangelist in John, and her witness is simple. Many Samaritans believe because of her word, and then they invite Jesus to stay two days. Then many more believe, and they say, “We know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.” The Gospel crosses the boundary of ethnicity.

Meanwhile the disciples are puzzled that Jesus has no need of food. He says, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me.” He points to the fields white for harvest.

Back in Cana, an official comes from Capernaum begging Jesus to heal his dying son. Jesus says, “Go; your son will live.” The man believes the word and goes, and finds that the fever left at the very hour. This is the second sign. Faith takes Jesus at his word.
connection: Genesis 29:1-12, Exodus 2:15-21, and Genesis 24 are Old Testament wells where significant meetings happen. Isaiah 12:3 and 55:1 promise water for the thirsty. Jeremiah 2:13 speaks of the fountain of living water. Ezekiel 47:1-12 pictures a river flowing from the temple. John 7:37-39 explains that the living water is the Spirit. Acts 8:4-25 records the gospel’s spread to Samaria. Revelation 21:6 and 22:17 offer the water of life freely.
application:
Think about what you drink from to satisfy your thirst, such as approval, success, or comfort. Bring it to Jesus.

Like the woman, tell someone simply what Jesus has done in your life.

Who is the Samaritan in your life, a person it would be awkward to talk to about Jesus? Ask God for a chance.
prayerPrompts: Tell Jesus that he knows everything about you, and let that be good news.
Ask him to teach you to tell others about him.
